title: Procalcitonin
subtitle: Bacterial infection marker and sepsis biomarker
summary: Procalcitonin (PCT) measurement for discrimination of bacterial from viral infection and assessment of sepsis severity.
introduction: Procalcitonin is a precursor of calcitonin produced by neuroendocrine cells in response to bacterial or fungal infection. It rises rapidly in sepsis but remains low in viral infection, making it useful for antibiotic stewardship. Levels correlate with sepsis severity.

rows.name: Procalcitonin
lowInterpretation: PCT <0.05 ng/mL: Viral infection or non-infectious cause likely. Antibiotics may be withheld if clinical picture supports viral illness.
PCT 0.05–0.25 ng/mL: Low probability of bacterial infection; not typical of sepsis. Close monitoring without antibiotics may be appropriate.
highInterpretation: PCT 0.25–0.5 ng/mL: Intermediate risk; bacterial infection or early sepsis possible. Clinical context and CRP inform antibiotic decision.
PCT >0.5 ng/mL: Bacterial infection or sepsis likely. Start antibiotics if clinical features support (fever, tachycardia, systemic illness).
PCT >2 ng/mL: Severe sepsis or septic shock likely. Immediate antibiotic therapy and intensive care assessment required.
notes: Rises within 6–12 hours of bacterial infection; peaks at 24 hours.
Also elevated in fungal infections, severe viral infections (dengue, malaria), malignancy, trauma, surgery.
Serial measurements show decline during appropriate therapy (24–48 hours) or persistent elevation if inadequate source control.
Renal failure and transplantation can elevate PCT despite absence of infection.

urgentFindings: PCT >0.5 ng/mL + fever + systemic illness: suspected sepsis; start antibiotics and investigation for source.
PCT >2 ng/mL + signs of shock: severe sepsis/septic shock; immediate antibiotics, fluid resuscitation, ICU.
PCT <0.05 ng/mL + no systemic illness: viral illness likely; antibiotics not indicated.
Serial PCT decline + clinical improvement: supports antibiotic de-escalation after 48–72 hours.
overrides: PCT should not delay antibiotics in acutely ill patients with suspected sepsis; use as adjunct to clinical judgement.
Elevated PCT does not indicate which antibiotic; culture and sensitivity drive specific choice.
Do not use PCT alone to diagnose infection; always integrate with fever, vital signs, WCC, CRP, and source findings.

commonPatterns.title: Fever with acute respiratory infection
interpretation: Likely viral URI or early infection
PCT helps discriminate viral from bacterial pneumonia
Low PCT suggests viral; high PCT suggests bacterial
actions: If PCT <0.1 ng/mL + normal CXR: viral illness, supportive care
If PCT >0.5 ng/mL + CXR infiltrate: bacterial pneumonia, antibiotics

commonPatterns.title: Fever without source (young child)
interpretation: PCT helps identify serious bacterial infection risk
Low PCT suggests lower bacteraemia risk
actions: If PCT <0.05 ng/mL: low bacteraemia risk, observation acceptable
If PCT >0.5 ng/mL + high fever: empiric antibiotics, investigation for UTI/bacteraemia

commonPatterns.title: Suspected sepsis (mixed clinical picture)
findings: Unclear if sepsis or other cause
interpretation: PCT helps confirm or exclude sepsis
actions: If PCT <0.1 ng/mL: sepsis unlikely, investigate other causes (stroke, hypoglycaemia)
If PCT >1 ng/mL: sepsis confirmed, start antibiotics and source control

rationale: PCT >0.5 ng/mL or fever with systemic illness
PCT elevated + fever without respiratory/abdominal source
≥80% drop or fall below 0.5 ng/mL supports de-escalation
